rich_summary: Victor works alone in his island laboratory finishing the female companion he promised the Creature. As the moon rises, he imagines the consequences: the new being might reject the Creature, become even more violent, or reproduce a race of monsters that could threaten humanity. Horrified by the moral weight of his promise, Victor suddenly sees the Creature watching through the window. In a surge of resolve he tears the unfinished body apart. The Creature responds with despair and fury, vowing revenge and delivering the ominous threat: he will be with Victor on his wedding night. Victor disposes of the remains at sea but is blown off course in a storm and lands in an unfamiliar town, where hostile locals accuse him of involvement in a recent murder—setting up the next catastrophe.

highlight_spans.why: Victor’s opening reflections reveal the ethical horror of repeating his creation and introduce the central dilemma: whether he has the right to risk unleashing another monster.
The pivotal moment when Victor sees the Creature watching him and destroys the unfinished female, permanently breaking his promise.
The Creature’s anguished speech about loneliness and revenge shows both his suffering and the terrifying depth of his hatred.
The iconic threat: the Creature promises to be with Victor on his wedding night, a line that drives the dread of the remaining chapters.
Victor casting the remains of the destroyed creature into the dark sea emphasizes guilt, secrecy, and the eerie atmosphere of the novel’s creation imagery.

top_scenes.scene_text: In the moonlit laboratory, Victor tears apart the half‑finished female creature while the original monster grins through the window and watches in silent fury.
The Creature confronts Victor in the dim room and delivers the chilling promise: 'I shall be with you on your wedding-night.'
Alone at night in a small skiff, Victor dumps a basket of dismembered body parts weighted with stones into the black sea as clouds swallow the moon.
